subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: The radius and height of a cylindrical water reservoir is 2.8 m and 3.5 m respectively. How much maximum water can the tank hold ? A person needs 70 litre of water per day. For how many persons is the water sufficient for a day ? \(\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\)
solution:
\(r = 2.8\) m, \(h = 3.5\) m, \(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\)

Capacity of the water reservoir = Volume of the cylindrical reservoir

\(= \pi r^2 h\)

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.8 \times 2.8 \times 3.5\)

\(= 86.24\ \text{m}^3\)

\(= 86.24 \times 1000\)   \((\because 1\ \text{m}^3 = 1000\ \text{litre})\)

\(= 86240.00\) litre.

\(\therefore\) the reservoir can hold 86240 litre of water.

The daily requirement of water of a person is 70 litre.

\(\therefore\) water in the tank is sufficient for \(\dfrac{86240}{70} = 1232\) persons.

ref: Surface area and volume of solids SolvedEx.2
subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: How many solid cylinders of radius 10 cm and height 6 cm can be made by melting a solid sphere of radius 30 cm ?
solution:
Radius of a sphere, \(r = 30\) cm

Radius of the cylinder, \(R = 10\) cm

Height of the cylinder, \(H = 6\) cm

Let the number of cylinders be \(n\).

Volume of the sphere \(= n \times\) volume of a cylinder

\(\therefore n = \dfrac{\text{Volume of the sphere}}{\text{Volume of a cylinder}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\frac{4}{3}\pi (r)^3}{\pi (R)^2 H}\)

\(= \dfrac{\frac{4}{3} \times (30)^3}{10^2 \times 6} = \dfrac{\frac{4}{3} \times 30 \times 30 \times 30}{10 \times 10 \times 6} = 60\)

\(\therefore\) 60 cylinders can be made.

subtopic: Combination of Solids and Frustum
stem: A tent of a circus is such that its lower part is cylindrical and upper part is conical. The diameter of the base of the tent is 48 m and the height of the cylindrical part is 15 m. Total height of the tent is 33 m. Find area of canvas required to make the tent. Also find volume of air in the tent.
solution:
Total height of the tent = 33 m.

Let height of the cylindrical part be H

\(\therefore\) H = 15 m.

Let the height of the conical part be \(h\)

\(\therefore h = (33 - 15) = 18\) m.

Slant height of cone, \(l = \sqrt{r^2 + (h)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{24^2 + 18^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{576 + 324}\)

\(= \sqrt{900}\)

\(= 30\) m.

Canvas required for tent = Curved surface area of the cylindrical part + Curved surface area of conical part

\(= 2\pi rH + \pi r l\)

\(= \pi r (2H + l)\)

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 24\,(2 \times 15 + 30)\)

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 24 \times 60\)

\(= 4525.71\ \text{m}^2\)

Volume of air in the tent = volume of cylinder + volume of cone

\(= \pi r^2 H + \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\)

\(= \pi r^2 \left(H + \dfrac{1}{3}h\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 24^2 \left(15 + \dfrac{1}{3} \times 18\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 576 \times 21\)

\(= 38{,}016\ \text{m}^3\)

\(\therefore\) canvas required for the tent \(= 4525.71\ \text{m}^2\)

\(\therefore\) volume of air in the tent \(= 38{,}016\ \text{m}^3\).

subtopic: Combination of Solids and Frustum
stem: A bucket is frustum shaped. Its height is 28 cm. Radii of circular faces are 12 cm and 15 cm. Find the capacity of the bucket. \(\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\)
solution:
[Textbook note: in the third line of the book's printed working the bracket is set as \((15^2 \times 12^2 + 15 \times 12)\); the correct expression is \((15^2 + 12^2 + 15 \times 12)\), which is what the book's own next line \((225 + 144 + 180)\) evaluates. The printed final answer is unaffected.]

\(r_1 = 15\) cm, \(r_2 = 12\) cm, \(h = 28\) cm

Capacity of the bucket = Volume of frustum

\(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h\left(r_1^{\,2} + r_2^{\,2} + r_1 \times r_2\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 28\,(225 + 144 + 180)\)

\(= \dfrac{22 \times 4}{3} \times 549\)

\(= 88 \times 183\)

\(= 16104\ \text{cm}^3 = 16.104\) litre

\(\therefore\) capacity of the bucket is 16.104 litre.
note: The book's printed solution sets the bracket as \((15^2 \times 12^2 + 15 \times 12)\) where a \(+\) belongs between the two squares; its own next line evaluates \((225 + 144 + 180)\), so the misprint is in the operator only.

stem:
The circumferences of circular faces of a frustum are 132 cm and 88 cm and its height is 24 cm. To find the curved surface area of the frustum complete the following activity. \(\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\).

circumference\(_1 = 2\pi r_1 = 132\)

\(r_1 = \dfrac{132}{2\pi} = \boxed{\quad}\)

circumference\(_2 = 2\pi r_2 = 88\)

\(r_2 = \dfrac{88}{2\pi} = \boxed{\quad}\)

slant height of frustum, \(l = \sqrt{h^2 + (r_1 - r_2)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{\boxed{\quad}^{\,2} + \boxed{\quad}^{\,2}}\)

\(= \boxed{\quad}\) cm

curved surface area of the frustum \(= \pi(r_1 + r_2)\,l\)

\(= \pi \times \boxed{\quad} \times \boxed{\quad}\)

\(= \boxed{\quad}\) sq.cm.

subtopic: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
stem: The measure of a central angle of a circle is 150\(^\circ\) and radius of the circle is 21 cm. Find the length of the arc and area of the sector associated with the central angle.
solution:
\(r = 21\) cm, \(\theta = 150\), \(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\)

Area of the sector, \(A = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2\)

\(= \dfrac{150}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 \times 21\)

\(= \dfrac{1155}{2} = 577.5\ \text{cm}^2\)

Length of the arc, \(l = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r\)

\(= \dfrac{150}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21\)

\(= 55\) cm

subtopic: Area of Combined Figures
stem: In figure 7.29, P is the centre of the circle of radius 6 cm. Seg QR is a tangent at Q. If PR = 12, find the area of the shaded region. \((\sqrt{3} = 1.73)\)
solution:
Radius joining point of contact of the tangent is perpendicular to the tangent.

\(\therefore\) in \(\triangle\) PQR, \(\angle\) PQR \(= 90^\circ\), PQ = 6 cm, PR = 12 cm \(\therefore\) PQ \(= \dfrac{\text{PR}}{2}\)

If one side of a right anglesd triangle is half the hypoteneus then angle opposite to, that side is of 30\(^\circ\) measure

\(\therefore \angle\) R \(= 30^\circ\) and \(\angle\) P \(= 60^\circ\)

\(\therefore\) by \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) theorem, QR \(= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times\) PR \(= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 12 = 6\sqrt{3}\)

\(\therefore\) QR \(= 6\sqrt{3}\) cm

\(\therefore \text{A}(\triangle \text{PQR}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\text{QR} \times \text{PQ}\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6\sqrt{3} \times 6\)

\(= 18\sqrt{3} = 18 \times 1.73\)

\(= 31.14\ \text{cm}^2\)

Area of a sector \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2\)

\(\text{A(P--QAB)} = \dfrac{60}{360} \times 3.14 \times 6^2\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{6} \times 3.14 \times 6 \times 6 = 3.14 \times 6\)

\(= 18.84\ \text{cm}^2\)

Area of shaded region = A(PQR) \(-\) A(P-QAB)

\(= 31.14 - 18.84\)

\(= 12.30\ \text{cm}^2\)

Area of the shaded region \(= 12.30\ \text{cm}^2\)
note: The book prints "anglesd" for "angled" and "hypoteneus" for "hypotenuse" — transcribed as printed. The stem states only \(\sqrt{3} = 1.73\); the printed working also uses \(\pi = 3.14\) without saying so.

subtopic: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
stem: In the figure 7.40, \(\angle\) AOB = 30\(^\circ\), OA = 12 cm . Find the area of the segment. \((\pi = 3.14)\)
solution:
**Method I**

\(r = 12\), \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\pi = 3.14\)

\(\text{A(O--AXB)} = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2\)

\(= \dfrac{30}{360} \times 3.14 \times 12^2\)

\(= 3.14 \times 12\)

\(= 37.68\ \text{cm}^2\)

\(\text{A}(\triangle \text{OAB}) = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2 \times \sin\theta\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12^2 \times \sin 30\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 144 \times \dfrac{1}{2}\)   \(\left(\because \sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\)

\(= 36\ \text{cm}^2\)

A(segment AXB) = A(O-AXB) \(-\) A(\(\triangle\) OAB)

\(= 37.68 - 36\)

\(= 1.68\ \text{cm}^2\)

**Method II**

A(segment AXB) \(= r^2\left[\dfrac{\pi\theta}{360} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{2}\right]\)

\(= 12^2\left[\dfrac{3.14 \times 30}{360} - \dfrac{\sin 30}{2}\right]\)

\(= 144\left[\dfrac{3.14}{12} - \dfrac{1}{2 \times 2}\right]\)

\(= \dfrac{144}{4}\left[\dfrac{3.14}{3} - 1\right]\)

\(= 36\left[\dfrac{3.14 - 3}{3}\right]\)

\(= \dfrac{36}{3} \times 0.14\)

\(= 12 \times 0.14\)

\(= 1.68\ \text{cm}^2.\)

subtopic: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
stem: The radius of a circle with centre P is 10 cm. If chord AB of the circle substends a right angle at P, find areas of the minor segment and the major segment. \((\pi = 3.14)\)
solution:
\(r = 10\) cm, \(\theta = 90\), \(\pi = 3.14\)

\(\text{A(P--AXB)} = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2\)

\(= \dfrac{90}{360} \times 3.14 \times 10^2\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 314\)

\(= 78.5\ \text{cm}^2\)

\(\text{A}(\triangle \text{APB}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\text{base} \times \text{height}\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10\)

\(= 50\ \text{cm}^2\)

A (minor segment) = A(P-AXB) - A(\(\triangle\) PAB)

\(= 78.5 - 50\)

\(= 28.5\ \text{cm}^2\)

A(major segment) = A(circle) \(-\) A(minor segment)

\(= 3.14 \times 10^2 - 28.5\)

\(= 314 - 28.5\)

\(= 285.5\ \text{cm}^2\)
note: The book prints "substends" for "subtends" — transcribed as printed.

subtopic: Area of Combined Figures
stem: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius 14 cm. Find the area of the region between the circle and the hexagon. \(\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7},\ \sqrt{3} = 1.732\right)\)
solution:
side of the hexagon = 14 cm

A(hexagon) \(= 6 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times (\text{side})^2\)

\(= 6 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 14^2\)

\(= 509.208\ \text{cm}^2\)

A(circle) \(= \pi r^2\)

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14\)

\(= 616\ \text{cm}^2\)

The area of the region between the circle and the hexagon

\(=\) A(circle) \(-\) A(hexagon)

\(= 616 - 509.208\)

\(= 106.792\ \text{cm}^2\)

Area of square = \((\text{side})^2 = \boxed{\quad}^{\,2} = \boxed{\quad}\) ..... (I)

Area of shaded region inside the square

= Area of square ABCD \(-\) Area of sector C-BXD

\(= \boxed{\quad} - \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2\)

\(= \boxed{\quad} - \dfrac{90}{360} \times \dfrac{3.14}{1} \times \dfrac{400}{1}\)

\(= \boxed{\quad} - 314\)

\(= \boxed{\quad}\)

Radius of bigger sector = Length of diagonal of square ABCD \(= 20\sqrt{2}\)

Area of the shaded regions outside the square

= Area of sector A-PCQ \(-\) Area of square ABCD

= A(A-PCQ) \(-\) A(\(\square\)ABCD)

\(= \left(\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi \times r^2\right) - \boxed{\quad}^{\,2}\)

\(= \dfrac{90}{360} \times 3.14\,(20\sqrt{2})^2 - (20)^2\)

\(= \boxed{\quad} - \boxed{\quad}\)

\(= \boxed{\quad}\)

\(\therefore\) total area of the shaded region = 86 + 228 = 314 sq.cm.

subtopic: Circumference of a Circle
stem:
In the figure 7.49, two circles with centres O and P are touching internally at point A. If BQ = 9, DE = 5, complete the following activity to find the radii of the circles.

Let the radius of the bigger circle be R and that of smaller circle be r.

OA, OB, OC and OD are the radii of the bigger circle

\(\therefore\) OA = OB = OC = OD = R

PQ = PA = r

OQ = OB \(-\) BQ = \(\boxed{\quad}\)

OE = OD \(-\) DE = \(\boxed{\quad}\)

As the chords QA and EF of the circle with centre P intersect in the interior of the circle, so by the property of internal division of two chords of a circle,

OQ \(\times\) OA = OE \(\times\) OF

\(\boxed{\quad} \times \text{R} = \boxed{\quad} \times \boxed{\quad}\) .......... \((\because\) OE = OF)

\(\text{R}^2 - 9\text{R} = \text{R}^2 - 10\text{R} + 25\)

R = \(\boxed{\quad}\)

AQ = 2r = AB \(-\) BQ

2r = 50 \(-\) 9 = 41

r = \(\boxed{\quad}\) = \(\boxed{\quad}\)
note: This is a chord-property question printed in the Mensuration problem set; none of the chapter's subtopics is a natural home for it, so it is filed under "Circumference of a Circle" (its answers are the radii of two circles).
